title: The Radiators of the fourth floor walk-up
premise: Ulyana Zhou, a bridge inspector who measures everything except his own heart, has spent seven years estranged from the family that took him in after his mother's death, practicing the art of almost saying what matters. At the funeral of Marisol, the matriarch of the fourth-floor walk-up, a stranger addresses him by 'Yanya'—a name only she ever used—revealing that Marisol left him letters and half-ownership of the building, and that the radiators he once repaired are failing along with the building itself. Returning to repair both, Ulyana uncovers the misunderstanding that drove him away: Marisol's son Dmitri never resented him; he was protecting Ulyana from a debt and a secret about his mother. As demolition notices arrive and winter closes in, Ulyana must finally say the unsaid—to Dmitri, to the neighbors who became family, and to himself—before the walk-up, and his last chance at belonging, comes down.
about_author: Ada Whitlock is a former structural engineer who spent a decade inspecting bridges across the Rust Belt before turning to fiction. She writes about the quiet mathematics of families and the places that hold them together.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. On a bridge inspection in Buffalo, Ulyana measures tolerances with obsessive precision while avoiding a call from home. The news arrives: Marisol is dead. He doesn't cry; he recalibrates an instrument twice. Emotional beat: grief deferred into work, the reader learns how he converts feeling into measurement.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. At the funeral, among the fourth-floor walk-up's tenants, a stranger greets him as 'Yanya.' No one else uses the name; it belonged to Marisol alone. The stranger, a lawyer named Okafor, mentions papers. Emotional beat: the shock of being known, and the first crack in seven years of practiced invisibility.

chapters.title: Half a Building
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. In Okafor's office, Ulyana learns Marisol left him half the walk-up and a shoebox of unopened letters addressed to 'Yanya.' He refuses at first, but signs anyway, telling himself it's temporary. Emotional beat: guilt disguised as obligation; the past acquires legal weight.

chapters.title: Dmitri Doesn't Look Up
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins with Dmitri. Ulyana returns to the fourth floor to meet co-heir Dmitri, who receives him with cold courtesy. The radiator in Marisol's old room clanks like a living thing. Neither man says what needs saying. Emotional beat: two men orbiting the same wound, unable to touch it.

chapters.title: Letters in Boiling Water
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Steam from the failing boiler warps the shoebox; Ulyana steams open the first letter and finds Marisol wrote to him every year he was gone. The letters reference something called 'the debt' and 'what happened to your mother.' Emotional beat: tenderness arriving too late, and the first real question—why did he leave?

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Know
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV through tenant Rosa. Rosa and the other tenants reveal fragments: Marisol borrowed against the building years ago to pay for something involving Ulyana's mother; Dmitri has been quietly covering payments ever since. A developer circles with buyout offers. Emotional beat: the building as a body of witnesses; belonging reasserting itself around Ulyana whether he wants it or not.

chapters.title: The Winter the Pipes Sang
chapters.summary: Dmitri's POV. A cold snap bursts a riser; Ulyana and Dmitri are forced to work side by side through the night, shutting valves and moving elderly tenants upstairs. In the dark, almost-conversations accumulate. Emotional beat: forced intimacy; the old family rhythm reasserting itself in shared labor.

chapters.title: The Debt
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The final letter reveals the truth: Marisol paid off the men who threatened Ulyana's mother, and Dmitri's coldness was protection—he feared Ulyana would learn how much had been sacrificed and vanish out of shame. Ulyana realizes his exile protected no one. Emotional beat: devastating clarity; the story he told himself collapses.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Dmitri's POV. The developer files to condemn the building; Okafor finds a flaw—the debt was never properly discharged, and the notice is built on it. But fighting means going public with Marisol's sacrifice. Ulyana stands before the tenants and, for the first time, speaks plainly: who he is, what was done for him, what he owes. Emotional beat: climax; the art of almost-saying ends mid-sentence, completed.

chapters.title: Bleeding the Radiators
chapters.summary: Shared POV, closing on Ulyana. Spring: the condemnation fails, the debt is settled, and Ulyana stays—not as penance but as choice. He and Dmitri bleed the radiators together, releasing trapped air until each one runs warm and quiet. He writes back to one of Marisol's letters and leaves it in the shoebox for whoever comes next. Emotional beat: resolution; warmth circulating through an old structure, memory kept not by silence but by tending.
